USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: The United States should escalate tariffs on China to maximum levels, covering all remaining Chinese imports not yet subject to tariffs. This will pressure China to negotiate on structural issues like intellectual property theft, forced technology transfer, and market access restrictions. The US economy is strong enough to absorb short-term costs while China faces greater structural vulnerabilities.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score is -1 (clear opportunity) because China is overextended and the US has leverage. The US has already imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese goods, covering about half of US-China trade, and China has retaliated with tariffs on $110 billion of US goods but is running out of room to match since it only imports $130 billion total from the US. China's retaliation capacity is nearly exhausted while the US can still tariff another $267 billion. The US economy is growing strongly while China's export-dependent economy faces greater risk. The action score is -1 (maximal escalation) because this is a rare moment of leverage: China cannot match further US escalation, the Trump administration has domestic political support heading into midterms, and the longer the US waits, the more China can diversify supply chains. Escalating now maximizes US bargaining position for eventual negotiations.
key_factors: US has tariffed $250B of Chinese imports (~50% of trade); can still tariff $267B more
China's retaliation nearly exhausted at $110B of $130B total US imports
US economy strong; China more vulnerable as export-dependent
No high-level negotiations scheduled; Trump admin sees trade war as midterm election winner
China accused of unfair trade practices: IP theft, forced tech transfer, market restrictions
Soybean prices down 20%; specific US sectors hurt but overall economy minor blip per Brookings

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should continue to retaliate proportionally against U.S. tariffs while signaling willingness to negotiate. Retaliation preserves leverage and demonstrates to domestic and international audiences that China will not capitulate to unilateral trade aggression. However, China should simultaneously keep diplomatic channels open and avoid actions that would permanently foreclose a negotiated settlement.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat score of +0.55 reflects the significant and escalating damage the trade war poses to China's export economy. As of mid-October 2018, the U.S. has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese imports (10% rate, set to rise to 25% at year-end), covering roughly half of all U.S.-China trade (Fox Business/Motley Fool analysis). President Trump has threatened to tariff the remaining ~$267 billion if China retaliates, which would cover 100% of bilateral trade. China has already retaliated on $110 billion of the $130 billion in U.S. goods it imports, meaning nearly all cards have been played on the Chinese side (Fox Business). The Brookings analysis notes that China's export sectors—smartphones, computers, tablets—are embedded in global value chains where China is the final assembler, meaning tariffs disrupt not just bilateral trade but integrated supply chains. Soybean prices have fallen 20%, directly hitting U.S. farmers but also signaling the depth of disruption. The SCMP analysis notes the U.S. trade deficit framing ($375 billion in 2017) gives the Trump administration a politically potent narrative that is hard to counter. China faces the risk that the 10% tariff rate will jump to 25% at year-end, creating additional uncertainty for exporters.

The action score of -1 (retaliate) is justified because: (1) China has already exhausted most of its retaliatory tariff space ($110B of $130B), so further measured retaliation signals resolve without dramatically escalating; (2) the Brookings analysis states it is 'unlikely that the Chinese leadership will cave in and do anything major,' and capitulation would set a precedent for future U.S. coercion; (3) China's offer to 'buy more products from the U.S. and open more markets' is already on the table, so retaliation now preserves negotiating leverage for the post-midterm period when Brookings suggests negotiations may resume; (4) the Trump administration views the trade war as a midterm election strategy, meaning pressure may ease after November 2018 elections, making it rational to hold firm through this period rather than concede under electoral pressure.
key_factors: U.S. tariffs on $250B of Chinese imports (half of bilateral trade), with threat to tariff remaining $267B
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in U.S. imports, nearly exhausting tariff retaliation capacity
Tariff rate set to rise from 10% to 25% at year-end 2018, creating additional uncertainty
Trump administration views trade war as midterm election strategy; pressure may ease post-November
China embedded in global value chains as final assembler; tariffs disrupt integrated supply chains
Soybean prices down 20%, signaling depth of agricultural sector disruption
No high-level negotiations currently scheduled; diplomatic off-ramp unclear until after U.S. midterms
